steps.why: The last line is the one that matters for melting. Most solids are built of separate molecules held to each other by weak forces, and melting only has to separate those molecules. Diamond has no molecules at all.
common_mistakes: Calling diamond a molecular solid. It has no separate molecules; the whole crystal is a single covalent network.
Writing that the carbon atoms are held by van der Waals forces. Those act between graphite's sheets; in diamond every carbon is covalently bonded to four others.
steps.memory_tip: One crystal, one network, every carbon bonded to four others.
steps.margin_note: Say there are no separate molecules; that sentence sets up the reason.

steps.why: Melting point measures the energy needed to loosen a solid enough for it to flow. For diamond that energy is the energy of the covalent bonds themselves, which is why its melting point is far above that of a molecular solid.
common_mistakes: Writing that only a few bonds break on melting. Melting a covalent network means breaking bonds throughout the crystal.
Saying the high melting point is caused by the hardness. Both the hardness and the high melting point follow from the same network of strong bonds; one is not the cause of the other.
steps.memory_tip: No molecules to separate, so the bonds themselves have to break.
steps.margin_note: Give the bond energy figure if you can; it makes the reason concrete.

insider_note: A complete answer says diamond is one giant covalent network with no separate molecules, so melting it means breaking strong C–C bonds throughout the crystal.
